stories.headline: Update: Paraguay's Ousted President Santiago Peña Placed Under House Arrest Over Ueno Bank Collapse
stories.summary:
Paraguay's former president, Santiago Peña, has been placed under house arrest on suspicion of breach of trust as prosecutors investigate the collapse of Ueno Bank, a popular lender. The detention follows his removal from office by the Senate on Friday. The lower house of Congress had earlier voted to pursue an impeachment trial against him.

Peña had previously been reported to have resigned amid the crisis linked to the bank's failure. The Senate's decision to remove him formally paves the way for potential criminal charges over his alleged role in the lender's collapse. Prosecutors are examining whether he breached the trust of his office in connection with the bank.

The sudden leadership change comes as Paraguay reels from the failure of Ueno Bank, which was widely used by ordinary savers. The episode is a serious political and financial shock for the country, and attention now turns to who will lead the government during the transition and how depositors will be protected. Further legal steps against Peña are expected as the investigation proceeds.

stories.headline: Update: Vance Leads Behind-the-Scenes Push for New Iran Ceasefire and Nuclear Talks
stories.summary:
Vice President JD Vance has spent the past two weeks personally involved in indirect talks with Iran aimed at securing a new ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations, according to Axios, citing two sources with knowledge of the matter. The sources said there is progress, but that it is moving extremely slowly.

Vance's involvement elevates the latest round of indirect talks to the highest levels of the administration. Axios reported that he is taking it upon himself to extract the United States from a conflict he has blamed for the Republican Party's heavy losses in this week's midterm elections. Vance has publicly put distance between himself and the president on the war, while President Trump has said he will soon decide whether to resume strikes, keep pressuring Iran economically, or pursue a deal.

The effort comes as Trump's administration enters a lame-duck phase with Democrats set to control Congress, and as Qatari mediators urge both sides not to wait for a perfect moment to reach an agreement. Supporters of a deal argue the war has become politically and economically costly, while hawks in the administration and party favor renewed military pressure. No timeline for an agreement has been announced.

stories.headline: Justice Department Drops Lawsuit Over 20,000 Disputed California Ballots
stories.summary:
The Justice Department on Friday asked a court to dismiss its own lawsuit seeking to force California election officials to set aside roughly 20,000 ballots that the federal government alleged were cast by non-citizens. The move ends a high-profile legal effort that had sought to stop the state from counting the votes.

The Supreme Court had already ruled against the Trump administration in an emergency order ahead of Election Day, blocking the effort. With that ruling in place and the votes now being counted, the department withdrew the case.

The administration argued the ballots belonged to voters who were not eligible to cast them, while California officials and Democrats called the effort baseless and an attempt to undermine the count. The dismissal arrives as vote tallying continues in close races nationwide after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress.

stories.headline: Sen. Chris Murphy to Miss 'Several Weeks' of Votes While Recovering From Stroke
stories.summary:
Sen. Chris Murphy, a Connecticut Democrat, said Friday he has been discharged from Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore after suffering a stroke last weekend. He will spend several weeks at a rehabilitation center and will miss the next several weeks of Senate votes.

The 53-year-old said doctors are encouraged by the progress he has made so far. His doctor said he expects Murphy to make a full recovery following rehabilitation.

The absence comes as the Senate returns for a lame-duck session next week, with Democrats having won control of the chamber in the midterm elections. Murphy's votes could matter in closely divided lame-duck business before the new Congress is seated in January.

stories.headline: Update: Judge Chutkan Blocks Trump's 250-Foot Arch Hours After Planning Commission Approval
stories.summary:
A federal judge issued a temporary restraining order halting construction of President Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, D.C. Judge Tanya Chutkan's ruling came less than two hours after the National Capital Planning Commission, a panel whose membership includes presidential allies, granted final approval to the project in an 8-4 vote.

The Trump administration had said it expected to begin construction immediately, possibly as early as this week. A Vietnam veteran leading the lawsuit to stop the project called the arch "frankly blasphemous" ahead of the commission vote. The restraining order temporarily pauses work while the court considers the legal challenge.

Supporters of the project, including the administration and its allies, have framed the arch as a fitting national monument and say the approval process was properly followed. Opponents argue the commission was stacked with loyalists and that the approval was rushed, raising procedural and legal questions about the process. Coverage from outlets across the spectrum, including Fox News, NPR, NBC, ABC and the BBC, has focused on the speed of the sequence of events.

The case will now proceed before Chutkan, who is weighing whether to extend the halt. The ruling is the first judicial check on the arch since the commission's approval, and a longer injunction would delay the administration's construction timeline.

stories.headline: Tanzanian Opposition Leader Tundu Lissu Convicted of Inciting Unrest, Acquitted of Treason
stories.summary:
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, was found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in prison. A three-judge panel of the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted the 58-year-old of the more serious charge of treason, which can carry the death penalty, saying prosecutors failed to prove a key element.

The court ruled that Lissu's campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was enough to support the incitement conviction, saying he intended to encourage the public to disrupt the 2025 general election. Lissu, who leads the Chadema party and has been detained since April last year, represented himself. He told the court the incitement offense was one the judges had "manufactured" on "political directives," and said he would seek bail, which is available for incitement but not for treason.

Amnesty International called the conviction a "travesty of justice." President Samia Suluhu Hassan won the October 2025 election with 98% of the vote after her two main challengers, including Lissu, were excluded; the opposition called the result a mockery of democracy. Her government has repeatedly denied targeting its opponents.

Lissu has leave to appeal to the Court of Appeal. If the four-year sentence is upheld, it would bar him from the next elections, due in 2030.

stories.headline: EU Prosecutors Open Fraud Probe at Spanish Rail Authorities After Urda Disaster
stories.summary:
European Union prosecutors have begun investigating the possible misuse of EU funds intended to upgrade the Spanish rail line where a crash killed 69 people last week. The European Public Prosecutor's Office said it was conducting investigative measures at the offices of the Adif infrastructure authority and the AESF rail safety agency, with support from a special unit of the Guardia Civil.

The inquiry concerns funds allocated to renovating safety, signalling and communications systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line. The 28 October collision near Urda, about 130 km south of Madrid, occurred when a Renfe train struck the back of a stationary Iryo train. The LZB system that monitors train positions had gone down, and the Renfe train was cleared to run at normal speed. It is the second EU fraud inquiry into Spanish railways this year, following the January Adamuz crash that killed 46 on the same line.

The disaster has damaged Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez's Socialist-led government ahead of the 29 November general election, in which it trails the conservative People's Party in most polls. Transport minister Oscar Puente resigned this week; the PP and far-right Vox say that is not enough and are demanding Sanchez resign. His successor, Carlos Cuerpo, met Adamuz survivors, who presented 11 demands. A funeral for the Urda victims will be held Tuesday at Toledo cathedral.

stories.headline: Congressional Democrats Plan Unified, Sustained Oversight of Trump Administration
stories.summary:
Congressional Democrats, preparing to take control of Congress, are working on a coordinated oversight strategy rather than the one-off hearings and subpoena threats that characterized their approach during Trump's first term. Senior Democrats say the goal is to build a sustained narrative around what they call the administration's "cost, chaos and corruption."

Democrats see what one account describes as a target-rich environment next year, but they are wary of overreach. Party strategists worry that if they investigate everything, they may appear to investigate nothing, diluting the message and giving Republicans an opening to portray the effort as partisan.

Republicans and administration allies have previously characterized Democratic investigations as political harassment, while Democrats argue oversight is a core constitutional duty of Congress. The planning comes as Republicans grapple with internal divisions after their midterm losses. Details on committee priorities and the timing of the first hearings are expected as the new Congress takes shape.

stories.headline: Trump Names Stephen Miller White House Chief of Staff, Replacing Susie Wiles After Midterm Losses
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump announced Friday that Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff. The change comes days after Republicans lost control of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections. Trump announced the move on his social media site, praising Wiles and saying she will continue working for his political organization.

Wiles, the first woman to hold the post, was the longest-serving chief of staff of Trump's tenure; during his first term he went through four. She released a statement calling her service "the honor of a lifetime" and citing the administration's work on border security, tax cuts and the economy. She said her commitment to "the President and the mission" will not change. Her departure follows her treatment for breast cancer, which she disclosed in March 2026 and said months later showed no evidence of disease.

Miller, currently deputy chief of staff, joined Trump's 2016 campaign as a speechwriter and is regarded as one of his closest and longest-serving advisers. A former aide to Jeff Sessions, he is considered a principal architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies. His elevation signals continuity on immigration as the White House prepares to work with a Democratic-controlled Congress.

The announcement is likely to draw differing reactions. Supporters view Miller as a loyal enforcer of the president's agenda, while critics are likely to see the move as a doubling down on contested immigration policy after an electoral rebuke. Neither the timing nor the reasoning behind the change was detailed beyond the statements from Trump and Wiles.

stories.headline: Update: Nvidia and Tech Shares Edge Up as Analysts Dissect $3.7 Trillion Post-Election Selloff
stories.summary:
US technology stocks showed signs of a partial recovery Friday after a sharp selloff following the midterm elections. On Thursday the Nasdaq composite closed down more than 5.5%, and Bloomberg estimated the rout wiped out $3.7 trillion in US market value in a single day. Other tallies put the loss in the Nasdaq alone at about $2.5 trillion.

When markets opened Friday, Nvidia's share price jumped more than 7%, and SpaceX rose about 6%. AMD and Micron also gained, though none had recovered their heavy losses from the previous day. Chipmakers and semiconductor firms closely tied to AI development took the hardest hits.

Investors had been selling in part over concerns that Democratic victories would mean tougher scrutiny of AI development, more regulation and restrictions on data center construction. A voter poll found data centers were a key issue for many Americans, and voters approved dozens of local data center moratoriums. Bloomberg noted that AI has been a boon to the stock market and the broader economy amid pressure from tariffs and the war in the Middle East, which raised the stakes of the selloff.

Market reporters cautioned that conditions can change quickly with a full day of trading ahead. Analysts continue to examine the chain reaction behind the drop, and its durability will depend on how the incoming Congress approaches AI policy.

stories.headline: Hegseth Authorizes National Guard to Expand D.C. Patrols With Military Vehicles, Boats and Rifles
stories.summary:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has approved an expanded National Guard presence in Washington, D.C., including military police cars, tactical vehicles and patrol boats, according to two memos signed Oct. 29 and obtained by The Associated Press. The memos authorize 60 military police cars, two patrol boats and 20 portable light towers to "enhance force protection in patrol zones." Troops will be allowed to carry rifles during some operations, though not in Metro rail stations.

The maximum number of deployed Guard members will remain at 3,500, below a summertime peak of about 5,000 during America's 250th anniversary celebrations. The memos require patrol cars to be marked "National Guard" and troops to be in uniform, and they forbid high-speed chases. Troops will play a greater role against "gangs and drug traffickers," with six analysts continuing to work on organized drug distribution in the city. One memo also grants the U.S. Marshals Service use of the D.C. National Guard's 260th Special Purpose Brigade.

President Donald Trump first deployed the Guard in the capital in August 2025 for what he called a crime-fighting mission. Guard members have since patrolled neighborhoods, dispersed homeless camps and assisted with citywide cleanup. The expansion comes amid a series of incidents involving deployed troops, including the arrest of a Georgia serviceman for pulling a gun on a fellow Guard member, the arrest of a Guard member for carrying an unauthorized firearm, and the shooting of a Guardsman who was trying to break up a fight.

Supporters of the deployment argue it deters crime and supports local police, while critics question its cost and effectiveness and object to the militarized appearance of the vehicles on city streets.

stories.headline: Jay Rockefeller, Former West Virginia Governor and U.S. Senator, Dies at 89
stories.summary:
Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family's political dynasty and the only Democrat in it to serve as West Virginia's governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, died Thursday night at his home in Washington. He was 89. The news was confirmed by Mary Stewart of WETA, the public broadcasting station where his wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.

Born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City, he came from one of the nation's wealthiest families, the great-grandson of Standard Oil founder John D. Rockefeller. He arrived in West Virginia in 1964 as a VISTA anti-poverty worker in the mining community of Emmons, an experience he said shaped every policy he pursued. Breaking with his family's Republican tradition, he won a seat in the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966, then served as secretary of state and two terms as governor.

His only political defeat came in the 1972 governor's race against Republican Arch A. Moore Jr. He later served 30 years in the U.S. Senate, retiring in 2015. Moore's daughter, Republican Shelley Moore Capito, won his Senate seat, and on Friday she called him "a true gentleman" whose friendship "transcended politics."

In his 2014 farewell speech, Rockefeller said he could not imagine "a more rewarding career" after a half century of public service in one of the nation's poorest states.

stories.headline: Thomas Markle Sr., Father of Meghan Markle, Arrested in Florida on Child Sexual Abuse Material Charges
stories.summary:
Thomas Markle Sr., the estranged father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday morning by federal agents outside Tampa, Florida, on charges related to child sexual abuse material, according to two people familiar with the matter who spoke to The Associated Press. Other reports describe a single count of possession of child pornography stemming from an FBI investigation into images allegedly stored on two devices.

The arrest follows reports by the British tabloid The Sun that Meghan's half brother, Thomas Markle Jr., found "hundreds, if not thousands" of such images in boxes at his father's former home in Cebu City, Philippines. Markle Jr. said he reported the material to Philippine police and contacted the FBI. Markle Sr., 82, was living in the Philippines earlier this year when he suffered a stroke and had a leg amputated, forcing his return to the United States.

Meghan Markle recently said she was "deeply distressed" by the allegations and revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about her father was sent to London police in 2018. She said her distance from him and her decision to bar contact with her children were meant to protect them.

The case now moves into the federal court process. Markle is presumed innocent unless proven guilty, and further details of the charges are expected to emerge.

stories.headline: Update: AI Stocks Rebound After Trillions Wiped From Market Values; Strong Jobs Report Adds Mixed Picture
stories.summary:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms climbed Friday after a sell-off on Thursday that wiped trillions of dollars from stock values. The Nasdaq Composite opened higher and was about 1.7% up by lunchtime, recovering part of Thursday's 5.5% fall. The S&P 500 rose about 0.9%, and the Dow moved into positive territory after a slightly lower open.

Nvidia, which lost more than 9% Thursday, settled around 4% higher. AMD and Micron, which each fell more than 17%, rebounded by about 12% and 8% respectively. Investors had been selling in part over concerns that Democratic midterm victories could slow AI development, as some Democrats campaigned for new AI rules. Government data added to the mixed picture, showing an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added in September.

Markets elsewhere fared worse. South Korea's Kospi closed down 6%, with chipmaker SK Hynix falling more than 10%, and main indexes in Germany, France and Spain ended lower. The UK's FTSE 100 fell 1.01% as traders also weighed the Bank of England's decision to raise interest rates and a signal of another possible increase.

Dan Coatsworth of AJ Bell called it a brutal week and said next week would show whether the tech trade is fighting back or faltering.

stories.headline: Kenyan Doomsday Cult Leader Paul Mackenzie Sentenced to 200 Years for Murdering 191 People
stories.summary:
A Kenyan court sentenced cult leader Paul Mackenzie to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people, all but one of them children. Mackenzie was convicted alongside 28 others of instructing followers to starve their children to death so they could "meet Jesus." Justice Diana Mochache said he bore the "primary criminal culpability" for ordering the fasts, in one of the world's deadliest episodes of cult activity.

The court imposed 100 years for homicide and another 100 years for offences related to starvation. Sentences within each category run concurrently, but the two sets run consecutively. Prosecutors had sought the death penalty, and the judge ruled the case met the threshold for its consideration. She declined to impose it, saying capital punishment would eliminate any prospect of rehabilitation. Kenya has not carried out an execution since 1987.

The 28 co-accused, including guards who enforced the fasting orders and gravediggers who helped conceal bodies, received sentences of up to 160 years. Justice Mochache called the killings "cold and calculated" and said the perpetrators showed no remorse. Followers had believed Mackenzie was "Jesus's mouthpiece," and those who opposed his teachings were beaten to death.

Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest near the Kenyan coast. He was convicted on 19 October and had pleaded not guilty, insisting nobody was forced to die. He still faces separate manslaughter and terrorism charges, which he denies.

stories.headline: Two Dead, Including a Child, After Bus Crash in Eastern France
stories.summary:
A bus crash in eastern France on Friday killed a child and a young adult and left three people in critical condition. The bus was traveling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed around 7:00 a.m. local time in the town of Lent, about 55 kilometers from the Swiss border. Mayor Yves Cristin said the bus left the road and hit a tree in a ditch.

The bus carried 43 passengers, including 15 children. Authorities identified the dead as a young girl, whose reported age varied, and an 18-year-old man. Thirteen others suffered minor injuries. More than 100 firefighters and 50 gendarmes responded, and medical helicopters took the seriously injured to a specialized hospital.

The Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor opened an investigation on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries. The driver was hospitalized and has not yet been questioned. Transport Minister Philippe Tabarot said initial tests found no alcohol or drugs. The mayor said there was some fog and the road was wet, but no major difficulties. Tabarot noted the bus did not operate exclusively on school routes, though many schoolchildren were aboard.

stories.headline: Musk Signals Tesla Will Wind Down Cybertruck Production in Texas
stories.summary:
Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at its Texas factory next year to make room for its self-driving Cybercab. He did not say whether Tesla will stop making the vehicle entirely or move production elsewhere. Lead engineer Wes Morrill appeared to suggest it was being discontinued, writing that the Cybertruck "lives on through Cybercab."

Responding to a fan lamenting that the truck would be discontinued, Musk replied "true," adding that the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time. The vehicle has long been a passion project for Musk, who called it the best product Tesla has made as recently as April.

The Cybertruck launched in 2023 after delays, and sales have been disappointing despite Musk's claim of 146,000 orders in 2019. Several recalls, including one in 2025 affecting more than 46,000 vehicles, added to its troubles. Prices rose from a promised level to $61,000 for a fully equipped model, and the 2026 Cyberbeast costs $102,000.

stories.headline: Update: Indonesia's Presidential Wiretapping Scandal Widens as Chief of Staff Is Sacked and Treason Probed
stories.summary:
Indonesian authorities are investigating possible treason after announcing that President Prabowo Subianto's phone conversations may have been spied on. Chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo, who is not related to the president, was arrested Tuesday with two senior police officers and was sacked from his post, to which he had been appointed last month. On Thursday evening police named a fourth suspect, Slamet Uliandi of the national police criminal investigation unit, who was not detained because of ill health after a stroke.

The suspects allegedly entered phone numbers, including the president's, into the police electronic surveillance system without a warrant or case report. Authorities believe the operation dates to 2025, when Listyo was national police chief, and say it also targeted politicians, journalists, NGO representatives and businesspeople. A presidential spokesperson said it could amount to treason, which carries life imprisonment or death, though Indonesia has not executed anyone in a decade.

The motive remains unclear. Some analysts see a widening rift between Prabowo and predecessor Joko Widodo, to whom Listyo is considered close. Police chief Suyudi Ario Seto said the probe is purely law enforcement and unrelated to rivalries.

stories.headline: Somalia's Supreme Court Rules President's Term Extension Unlawful, Voids Chief Justice's Dismissal
stories.summary:
Somalia's Supreme Court ruled on Thursday that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, deepening a confrontation between the presidency and the judiciary. The ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed, a move the court declared "null and void" on the grounds that the president lacked the authority to take it. The president has appointed Ibrahim Idle Suleiman, who previously held the post, as a replacement.

Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through legal changes approved by parliament in March. The court held that the constitutional changes cannot be applied retrospectively to his current term. It ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and to hold elections within 90 days, which could upend government plans for nationwide polls next year. The electoral commission has scheduled parliamentary elections for 15 April 2027 and a presidential vote a month later, a timetable rejected by opposition groups and the regional administrations of Puntland and Jubaland.

The presidency said the dismissal followed complaints about the administration of justice and was meant to achieve a transparent judiciary. Mohamud argues his reforms are needed to move Somalia toward direct elections, replacing the clan-based system in which elders pick representatives. Opposition groups accuse him of using the changes to prolong his rule. Former President Sharif Sheikh Ahmed welcomed the ruling and urged a consensus approach, while former Prime Minister Hassan Ali Khaire accused the president of sending security forces to the court and trying to arrest the chief justice. AFP could not verify that claim, though photographs in Somali media appeared to show armed personnel inside the compound.

The crisis comes in a country that has not held nationwide direct elections since 1969 and where al-Shabaab still controls many rural areas.

stories.headline: Three States Carry Out Executions in One Day as Florida Ties Annual Record
stories.summary:
Florida, Indiana and Alabama each carried out an execution on the same day, a rare occurrence last seen before this year in 2010. Florida executed Jesse Guardado, 64, by three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke, with death pronounced at 6:13 p.m. It was the state's 19th execution of the year, tying its record. Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing 75-year-old Jackie Malone in her Walton County home in 2004.

Hours earlier, Indiana executed a man for killing two children in a 2010 house fire, and Alabama carried out the last lethal injection of the day for the killing of an elderly man and woman during a home robbery in 1991. It was the second time since August that three states executed prisoners on a single day. The U.S. has carried out 35 executions this year, more than half of them in Florida, and capital punishment has faced renewed scrutiny after Tennessee's failed execution of Christa Pike in September.

The executions came as California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he will commute all 548 death sentences in his state, saying "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California's values." Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a Republican, has signed the warrants for the state's record pace and says he wants to bring justice to victims' families who have often waited decades. Florida will set a new record if two more executions planned later this year proceed. Patrick Malone, the victim's son, questioned opponents of the death penalty, asking whether they consider the aftermath victims' families endure.

stories.headline: Update: Satellite Images Show Iran Rebuilding and Digging Near Missile Bases
stories.summary:
Iran appears to be undertaking significant new construction near at least two major missile sites and repairing bases damaged in months of US and Israeli air strikes, according to analysis of November satellite imagery. Analysts at the British intelligence firm MAIAR, speaking to BBC Verify, pointed to digging and new buildings at the Garmdareh base in Karaj near Tehran and the Shahroud base in the north. At least 12 other military sites show signs of repair.

At Kermanshah, new roofs have been built on destroyed buildings, and debris has been cleared at the Parchin complex, which has been repeatedly repaired despite successive strikes. Analysts said work at Parchin's Taleghan 2 facility includes a repaired underground bunker reinforced with concrete. Researchers at the Foreign Policy Research Institute said Karaj appears to show a new portal for an underground facility. Former CIA analyst Jim Lamson said the Shahroud excavations could relate to missile production, with the Revolutionary Guards probably seeking to move production underground.

The findings come as speculation grows that the US could resume attacks on Iran after this week's midterm elections. Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that the war's unpopularity cost Republicans in the vote and may have cost the party Senate control for six years. Earlier this week US officials described strikes on Qeshm Island as limited and defensive, and President Trump has acknowledged the war's role in the Republican defeat while defending his decision to launch it. Iranian parliament speaker Mohammed Bagher Ghalibaf has publicly endorsed a message tied to the conflict, and the administration is weighing a deal or renewed strikes.

stories.headline: Nigerian Court Invalidates Opposition Candidate Atiku Abubakar's Nomination
stories.summary:
Nigeria's Federal High Court in Abuja has removed the leadership of the opposition African Democratic Congress and ruled that the nomination of its presidential candidate, former Vice President Atiku Abubakar, is invalid. Justice Peter Lifu issued the judgment Thursday in a case brought by former ADC deputy chairman Nafiu Bala Gombe, who argued that interim chairman David Mark and others had not been elected at a national convention. Gombe said he should have taken over after the previous chairman resigned in 2025.

The ADC called the ruling a calculated attempt to cripple the opposition and said it will appeal. Abubakar, 79, said the decision showed the "panic was real" among those threatened by his candidacy, noting it came a day after a large crowd welcomed him at his campaign launch in Sokoto. He questioned why a new case reopened a dispute a different judge settled in July, when Justice Musa Liman found Mark was chosen lawfully.

Presidential elections are scheduled for 16 January, with President Bola Tinubu facing challengers including Abubakar and former Anambra governor Peter Obi. The electoral commission has issued its final candidate list, which includes Abubakar with former Rivers State governor Rotimi Amaechi as running mate. The ADC is seen as the strongest opposition vehicle, having drawn many influential politicians opposed to Tinubu's ruling All Progressives Congress. The legal fight could create uncertainty for the ticket and for ADC candidates in other races as the appeal proceeds.
